                                                        Abstract
     We study optimization with an approximate zero order oracle where there is a cost c() associated
     with querying the oracle with  accuracy. We consider the task of reconstructing a linear function:
     given a linear function f : X ⊆ Rd → [−1, 1] defined on a not-necessarily-convex set X, the goal is
     to reconstruct fˆ such that |f (x) − fˆ(x)| ≤  for all x ∈ X. We show that this can be done with cost
     O(d · c(/d)). The algorithm is based on a (poly-time computable) John-like theorem for simplices
     instead of ellipsoids, which may be of independent interest.
          This question is motivated by optimization with threshold queries, which are common in
     economic applications such as pricing. With threshold queries, approximating a number up to
     precision  requires c() = log(1/). For this, our algorithm has cost O(d log(d/)) which matches
     the Ω(d log(1/)) lower bound up to log factors.


1. Introduction
It is often the case that in order to evaluate a function f (·) you need to perform a costly procedure
such as solving an optimization problem or taking the average of many samples of a random variable.
In such scenarios, it tends to be possible to trade-off between accuracy and cost. Some examples (in
the following examples, we assume f (x) ∈ [−1, 1]):

    • if f (x) = E[Z(x)] and we can only sample Z(x) we can get an ε approximation of f (x) with
      1 − δ probability by taking the average of O(ε−2 log(1/δ)) samples.

    • if f (x) = miny∈Y g(x, y) for g(x, ·) is convex, we compute f (x) by minimizing g(x, ·) via a
      variant of gradient descent, we can an ε approximation of f in O(1/εα ) where the constant α
      depends on the properties of g (smooth vs non-smooth) and on the algorithm used (accelerated
      or not).

    • if we have access only to threshold queries, i.e., we can only ask if f (x) ≤ p or not, then we
      can get an ε-approximation of f using O(log(1/ε)) queries.

    • if we have access to threshold queries, but we need to choose the thresholds in a non-adaptive
      manner (i.e., choose all the thresholds at the same time) then we can get an ε-approximation
      using O(1/ε) queries.

Oracle model In our model we will assume that a function f : X ⊂ Rd → [−1, 1] is equipped
with an oracle that given x ∈ X and ε > 0 returns y ∈ R such that |f (x) − y| ≤ ε (note that we only
allow queries to points in X and not more generally to points in Rd ). Each such query to the oracle
has some cost c(ε), where the function c(ε) depends on the underlying model (for example, for
threshold queries, c(ε) = log(1/ε); for stochastic zeroth order queries, c(ε) = ε−2 ). For simplicity
we will assume that c(ε) satisfies c(O(ε)) = O(c(ε)) (this holds for all polynomial/sub-polynomial
c(ε)).
Learning task We will consider the task of reconstructing a linear function. Assume f : X →
[−1, 1] is linear (with X not necessarily convex). Our goal is to produce a function fˆ : X → R such
that
                                     |f (x) − fˆ(x)| ≤ ε, ∀x ∈ X
    Our initial motivation for studying this problem is how to learn customer preferences through
pricing queries. Assume a point x ∈ X corresponds to a product represented by a vector of features.
We can interact with the customer by offering product x ∈ X at price p ∈ R and observing if the
customer purchases it or not. This corresponds to a threshold query. How many queries are necessary
to reconstruct the customer’s preference?
    While one main application is in pricing, threshold queries are also common in other domains
such as reliability testing (given a certain force, will a material break or not) and determining
effectiveness of drugs/vaccines (given a certain dose of a medication, will the patient be cured). In
such cases, there is usually a threshold separating the success and failure cases and the feedback is
binary.
Main Results and Techniques The natural approach for reconstructing f (x) = hv, xi is to choose
d points x1 , . . . , xd that are linearly independent in X, use our costly zero-order oracle to obtain an
estimate of f (xi ) for each xi , and then write x in the basis given by xi to compute f (x) for any x.
Indeed, if we choose each xi to be the unit vector ei (under the assumption ei ∈ X), this method
works – by measuring each f (ei ) to within ε/d, we can reconstruct f (x) for any x ∈ [0, 1]d to within
ε, for a total cost of dc(ε/d).
     This problem becomes harder when our set X of valid queries does not necessarily contain a
“good” basis like the unit vectors ei . The difficulty with this idea is that if the matrix with rows xi
is ill-conditioned, the error can be blown up by the condition number of the matrix, which can be
arbitrarily bad if the choice of xi is naive. The problem can therefore be thought of as follows: given
an arbitrary (not even necessarily convex) set X, how can we find a good basis for X?
     We begin by examining the case where X is convex. By measuring along the basis formed by the
axes of the John ellipsoid of X, we show it is possible to reconstruct f (x) with total cost dc(ε/d1.5 ).

Theorem 1 If X is convex, there is an efficient (polynomial-time) procedure with cost O(d ·
c(ε/d1.5 )) for reconstructing a linear function with a costly zero order oracle.

    We then consider the case where X is not-necessarily convex: for example, an arbitrary point set,
or the union of several convex bodies (here we assume we have access to X through an oracle that
given a vector w ∈ Rd returns a point x ∈ argmaxx∈X hw, xi). In this setting we can no longer use
the same strategy of Theorem 1 of measuring along the axes of the John ellipsoid of (the convex hull
of) X, since not all points in the convex hull of X can be directly queried.

    To overcome this difficulty, we design a variant of John’s theorem for simplices, showing that for
any set of points X, it is always possible to efficiently find a simplex T whose vertices are contained
in X such that a poly(d)-dilation of T contains X. This theorem is the main technical result of the
paper, and may be of independent interest.
Theorem 2 Given a (not necessarily convex) set X there is a polynomial time algorithm that selects
a simplex T with vertices in X such that X is contained in a translate of −4dT .
    By measuring along the basis formed by the vertices of this simplex, we show it is possible
to efficiently reconstruct f (x) with total cost dc(ε/d) (note that this is a strict improvement over
Theorem 1).
Theorem 3 For any (not necessarily convex) set X, there is an efficient (polynomial-time) procedure
with cost O(d · c(ε/d)) for reconstructing a linear function over X with a costly zero order oracle.
    Finally, we show that for the specific case of threshold queries where c(ε) = log ε−1 , we show
that these algorithms are nearly optimal: both algorithms incur total cost O(d log(d/ε)), but there
is an information-theoretic lower bound showing that any algorithm must incur total cost at least
Ω(d log(1/ε)) even when X is just the unit d-dimensional ball (Lemma 18). For other cost functions
mentioned above (e.g. c(ε) = ε−1 and c(ε) = ε−2 ), the above algorithms are optimal up to a
polynomial factor in d – understanding how to close this gap is an interesting open question.

1.1. Related Work
The geometric techniques we use for the reconstruction problem are closely related to the largest
simplex problem introduced by Khachiyan (1995) and recently studied by Summa et al. (2014) and
Nikolov (2015), who show approximation algorithms for maximum volume problem. Instead of
the volume, we work here with with a local notion of optimality: we look for simplices where it is
impossible to improve the volume by an α factor by changing any single vertex.
    Learning from threshold queries is a prominent component of much recent work in revenue opti-
mization and contextual pricing Cohen et al. (2016); Javanmard and Nazerzadeh (2016); Javanmard
(2017); Mao et al. (2018); Paes Leme and Schneider (2018); Shah et al. (2019). Unlike in this paper,
the majority of this work focuses on settings where we cannot query arbitrary points x, but instead
where a stream of points x1 , x2 , . . . are generated online (either stochastically or adversarially)
and the learner is only allowed to query those. Moreover, the typical objective is revenue and not
reconstruction.

4. Lower bounds
The cost of the procedure given in Lemma 5 is nearly optimal for threshold queries with cost
c(ε) = O(log(1/ε)). For these queries, the procedure has cost O(d log(d/ε)) while no algorithm
can obtain better than Ω(d log(1/ε)) by a simple information theoretic argument sketched in the
following lemma.

Lemma 18 Any reconstruction procedure must incur cost at least Ω(d log(1/ε)) for threshold
queries, i.e., for c(ε) = log(1/ε).

Proof Let X be the ball of radius 1. We will construct k = (1/ε)Ω(d) linear functions fi (x) = vi> x
with fi (x) = vi> x such that maxx∈X |fi (x) − fj (x)| > ε. To do that observe that we can choose
k = (1/ε)Ω(d) points v1 , . . . , vk with kvi k = 1 such that kvi − vj k2 > ε for any i 6= j (using
standard ε-net arguments).
    Note that maxx∈X |fi (x) − fj (x)| = kvi − vj k2 > ε. For this reason, the reconstruction
algorithm must be able to distinguish between all functions fi . Since the cost of the query for
c(ε) = log(1/ε) corresponds to the number of bits needed to represent the result (in particular,
consider the implementation of this oracle which returns the answers to the log(1/ε) threshold
queries binary search would perform), we must need at least log((1/ε)O(d) ) = O(d log(1/ε)) total
cost.

    Against deterministic, non-adaptive algorithms, we can show a similar lower bound of Ω(dc(10ε))
for any cost function c. (Note that all our algorithms in Sections 2 and 3 are deterministic and non-
adaptive).

Lemma 19 Any deterministic non-adaptive reconstruction procedure must incur cost at least
Ω(dc(10ε)).

Proof Again, let X be the ball of radius 1 in Rd . Note that any deterministic and non-adaptive
algorithm must always make the same set of queries to the oracle; let us write these queries as
(x1 , ε1 ), (x2 , ε2 ), . . . , (xn , εn ), where (xi , εi ) means that the algorithm queries the oracle for the
value of f (xi ) to within error εi . Let k be the number of queries i where εi ≤ 10ε (and without
loss of generality, let these k queries be (x1 , ε1 ) through (xk , εk )). We will prove that we must have
k ≥ d, from which the theorem follows.
     Assume k < d. We will construct an instance on which this reconstruction procedure fails.
Specifically, we will show how to construct two linear functions f and f 0 and a sequence of responses
yi to the queries such that:

    • For each i, |yi − f (xi )| ≤ εi and |yi − f 0 (xi )| ≤ εi .

    • There exists an x ∈ X such that |f (x) − f 0 (x)| > 2ε.

     The first condition guarantees the response yi to query (xi , εi ) is valid for both functions f
and f 0 . The second condition guarantees that any correct reconstruction procedure must be able to
distinguish between these two functions.
     Consider the k points x1 , x2 , . . . xk . Since k < d, these points lie on some hyperplane H of
dimension d0 < d. Choose a unit vector u that is perpendicular to H. Consider the two linear
functions f (x) = 2εhu, xi and f 0 (x) = −2εhu, xi. Note that |f (u) − f 0 (u)| = 4ε, satisfying the
second point above. In addition, note that |f (x)| ≤ 2ε and |f 0 (x)| ≤ 2ε for all x.
     Now consider what happens if we set yi = 0 for all i (i.e. our oracle always responds 0). For
i ≤ k, note that f (xi ) = f 0 (xi ) = 0 (since xi ∈ H), so |yi − f (xi )| = |yi − f 0 (xi )| = 0, and
the first condition is satisfied. On the other hand, for i > k, we know that εi > 10ε, and therefore
|f (x) − yi | = |f (x)| ≤ εi (and likewise, |f 0 (x) − yi | ≤ εi ), and again the first condition is satisfied.
This implies the theorem statement.


5. Open Problems
In this paper, we demonstrate an algorithm which solves the reconstruction problem for arbitrary sets
with total cost O(dc(ε/d)). This is nearly tight for threshold queries (where c(ε) = log 1/ε), but not
necessarily for other cost functions. The main question left open is whether it is possible to improve
the asymptotic total cost of our algorithms, possibly to the lower bound of Ω(dc(ε)) in Lemma 19.
    One approach for improving our algorithms is to improve the O(d) bound in our analogue of
John’s theorem (Theorem 2). For simplices it turns out that this bound is asymptotically tight (see
Section 5.1 below), but we can ask the same question for convex combinations of larger numbers of
points.

    Finally, all of the algorithms presented in Sections 2 and 3 are deterministic and non-adaptive

reconstruction using a costly zero-order oracle? In particular, when the domain is either the ball or

5.1. John’s theorem for simplices with positive dilation
Theorem 2 states that in any set of S points in Rd , it is possible to find d + 1 points forming a simplex
T such that S is contained in a translate −O(d)T . Note that this requires a negative dilation factor.
Although it does not immediately help design better algorithms for the reconstruction problem, it is
natural to ask what is possible if we restrict ourselves to positive dilations only. Immediately, from
the fact that −T is contained within a translate of dT for any simplex T , Theorem 2 implies it is
possible to find a simplex T such that S is contained in a translate of O(d2 )T . Interestingly, it is
unclear if it is possible to do better.
